b:
I am struck by the need of Boglehead disciples to pay homage to one of their most revered commandments: “Thou shalt not trade.” But those brethren who choose to rebalance into stock funds when they “believe” the market is "down" and revert back to bonds when it is judged to be "up" are in fact trading.
It is, of course, true that buying low and selling high can be outrageously profitable. But for people who are (let’s face it) merely guesstimating whether the market will continue down or will reverse course, “rebalancing” is just a euphemism for trading. I am not referring here to day trading or swing trading or any other short-term merriment, but trading nonetheless.
It’s not that rebalancing doesn’t work-- much evidence indicates that it does. Over time, what starts as a tiny edge measurably enhances capital appreciation.
But that's not the point, which is simply that it is one of the very few effective trading approaches yet unearthed. So why do so many of that breed of worshipper bend their knee to the alter of rebalancing and rebuke the unrepentant trader? Psychologists have found that true believers are compelled to repeat the gospel to suppress an underlying fear of its limitations. Parishioners who “rebalance” when they divine the market has either “peaked” or “bottomed” are contortionists. The overdriven distortion that they are rebalancing when in fact they are just executing a time-tested trading strategy could be viewed as mildly delusional.
None of my high school English teachers ever mistook me for a budding Shakespearian scholar. But to paraphrase that perceptive bard, “Thou doth protest too much, me thinks.”
